activity.title: fix: generate long sources section by section
activity.body:
Depends on #838 and #839. This branch includes their commits; the last 4 commits are this PR.

## Problem

A long source produces about as many pages as a short one. A 2.8 MB trading textbook gave 11 pages besides its summary, while a 0.45 MB book gave 52. Nine of the 15 rows in the textbook summary's chapter map linked nothing, and common topics such as RSI, MACD, Bollinger Bands and position sizing had no page.

The cause is the funnel. Chunked analysis keeps one global digest, trimmed to 15,000 characters with at most 25 entities and 25 concepts. A single generation call then writes every page, and its prompt says the digest is authoritative for page decisions. So the page count is capped by the digest, whatever the length of the source.

## Changes

1. **Generate long sources section by section** (`fc98abb`). When a source needs chunked analysis, consecutive chunks are grouped into sections that fit the source budget. Each section gets its own generation call with the section's text and chunk notes, plus the digest for consistent names.
   - Each pass writes its pages before the next one starts. Through #839's list of pages already generated from this source, later passes see those pages and extend them instead of creating duplicates.
   - The final call works as before and writes the source summary and log entry. It runs last, so the summary can link to every page.
   - Section passes don't write the summary, log or review blocks.
   - If a pass reaches its output limit, it continues with the pages it hasn't written yet, up to 4 rounds per section.
   - Progress is saved after each section, so a failed or cancelled ingest resumes from the next section.
   - Sources that fit in one pass are unchanged.
2. **List a source's pages on its summary** (`7f03220`). After writing, the summary gets a "Pages From This Source" section, grouped by folder, with every page from this ingest that it doesn't already link. A later run rebuilds the section, so its entries stay unique. I added this because in one run the model's summary linked only 24 of a book's 450 pages, which left most of them unattached to the book in the graph.
3. **Merge into an existing page with the same file name** (`704cae1`). Wikilinks resolve by file name, so `concepts/volume-spike.md` and `indicators/volume-spike.md` make `[[volume-spike]]` ambiguous. Two section passes created exactly that pair. A new page whose file name already exists in another folder is now merged into the existing page.
4. **Don't import a file whose content is already in sources** (`741da27`). Ingest knows a source by its path. Re-importing a folder after renaming one of its files there, or picking the same file again (saved as `name (1)`), ingested the book a second time as a new source. For a long book that's an hour of calls. It also made a second summary page, and the second run couldn't see the first run's pages through #839, so it created near-duplicate pages under new names. Re-importing a folder also re-queued every file.
   - Before copying, the file is compared by MD5 with existing sources of the same size. A match isn't copied, and the import reports it as already in sources.
   - If the existing copy was never ingested (for example after a failed run), it's queued instead, so importing again still retries it.

## Real-model runs

All runs used the same model and the same schema.

**One textbook in an empty wiki (2.8 MB, 47 chunks, 1M context):**

| | Before | With this PR |
|---|---:|---:|
| Pages besides the summary | 11 | 453 |
| Chapters that link to pages | 6 of 15 rows | 24 of 24 |

That run had no broken frontmatter, no dead links and no ingest warnings. It took 77 minutes.

**Four long books together (0.3 to 2.8 MB):** they produced 450, 108, 106 and 40 pages, with no write warnings. The runs revealed the two problems that commits 2 and 3 fix: the summary that linked only 24 of 450 pages, and the volume-spike pair. Those two commits are covered by unit tests but haven't had a full real-model run yet.

## Cost and limits

- **Many more LLM calls for long sources.** There's one generation call per section, about 10 for the textbook at a 1M context, and more at smaller contexts. Each pass also lists the wiki's pages for #839, which reads every page. I haven't timed that on a large wiki.
- **A corrected long source doesn't replace its pages.** #838 replaces pages owned only by a changed source. For chunked sources that's turned off, because a later pass would replace what an earlier pass of the same run just wrote. Old wording can therefore survive on merged pages. The code marks this as a known shortcut.
- **The own-page list is capped.** #839 caps the list of this source's pages at 32,000 characters, which is about 400 pages for the textbook. Past that, a pass sees only part of the list.
- **Big summaries.** The textbook's summary carries about 450 links.
- **Import hashes files.** A file is hashed only when an existing source has the same size, but re-importing a large folder then reads both copies of every file. I haven't timed it.
- **Same name means same page.** Two genuinely different topics that end up with the same file name are now merged. Before, they coexisted with ambiguous links.

## Testing

- **New `autoIngest` tests:**
  - section text goes to the right pass, and later passes see earlier pages
  - the final pass lists every page, and section log blocks are ignored
  - a pass continues after hitting its output limit
  - a failed section resumes without repeating finished sections
  - a changed source's final pass doesn't replace a section's page
  - pages are listed on the summary, and the list is rebuilt on later runs
  - a page with an existing file name is merged into the existing page
- **New import tests:** a renamed copy in a folder import is skipped, a never-ingested existing copy is queued instead, a same-size file with different content is still imported, and picking the same file again doesn't make a numbered copy.
- **Unit test** for grouping chunks into sections.
- **Each test fails** when I disable the behaviour it covers.
- **Mock suite and `npm run typecheck`** pass on this branch.

activity.title: Linux: startup panic in libappindicator-sys when libayatana-appindicator3 is not installed
activity.body:
## Summary

On Linux, llm-wiki 0.6.13 panics during startup (`libappindicator-sys`: "Failed to load ayatana-appindicator3 or appindicator3 dynamic library") when the system does not have `libayatana-appindicator3` / `libappindicator3` installed. The process keeps running (API and clip servers still come up), but the system tray icon is never created and the panic appears at every launch. The dependency should either be declared/bundled by packaging, or the tray load failure should degrade gracefully instead of panicking the main thread.

## Environment

- App version: 0.6.13 (pacman package `llm-wiki-bin 0.6.13-1`)
- OS: Tacit 1.2.11 (Arch Linux–based, pacman)
- Kernel: Linux 7.2.7-1-cachyos #1 SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC x86_64 GNU/Linux (`linux` package 7.2.11.arch1-1)
- Desktop: Hyprland (session `Tacit:Hyprland`), locale `en_US.UTF-8`
- GTK: `gtk3 3.24.52`
- WebKit: `webkit2gtk-4.1 2.54.2`
- `libayatana-appindicator`: **not installed** at the time of the crash (fixed afterwards with `pacman -S libayatana-appindicator`, package version `0.6.1-1` in `extra`)

## Reproduction

1. Install llm-wiki 0.6.13 on an Arch-based system without `libayatana-appindicator` present.
2. Launch `llm-wiki` from a terminal.

## Expected Behavior

The app starts without panicking — either the tray icon works, or the app logs a warning and continues without it.

## Actual Behavior

The app panics during tray initialization; the panic shows up in the terminal before/alongside normal startup messages, and the tray icon is missing for that session:

```
[proxy] reading from /home/…/.local/share/com.llmwiki.app/app-state.json
[proxy] no proxyConfig in store, requests go direct

thread 'main' (120498) panicked at /home/runner/.cargo/registry/src/index.crates.io-1949cf8c6b5b557f/libappindicator-sys-0.9.0/src/lib.rs:41:5:
Failed to load ayatana-appindicator3 or appindicator3 dynamic library
libayatana-appindicator3.so.1: cannot open shared object file: No such file or directory
libappindicator3.so.1: cannot open shared object file: No such file or directory
libayatana-appindicator3.so: cannot open shared object file: No such file or directory
libappindicator3.so: cannot open shared object file: No such file or directory
note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace

[API Server] Listening on http://127.0.0.1:19828/api/v1
[Clip Server] Listening on http://127.0.0.1:19827
```

Also visible at startup, probably unrelated: `(llm-wiki:120498): Gtk-WARNING **: Unknown key gtk-hint-font-metrics in /usr/share/tacit/xdg/gtk-3.0/settings.ini`

## Additional Context

- On Arch, the fix on the user side is `pacman -S libayatana-appindicator` — after that the tray icon works.
- The panic originates in `libappindicator-sys 0.9.0` (from the crate compiled into this build). Ideally, either (a) the tray feature is made optional at runtime and logs a warning instead of panicking the main thread when the dynamic library can't be loaded, (b) the library is vendored/bundled with the released binaries, or (c) the package metadata declares it so dependency-aware package managers (pacman on Arch-based distros, via AUR or upstream `.deb` metadata) can pull it in. For reference, the pacman package this came from declares `Depends On: glibc webkit2gtk-4.1 libgcc glib2 gtk3 gdk-pixbuf2 xz libsoup3 hicolor-icon-theme cairo` — no appindicator — which is why the dependency ended up missing.

activity.title: feat: make side panels freely resizable
activity.body:
## Problem

The left sidebar stopped at 400px and the right panel at 50% of the window, so long file names and wide previews couldn't be given more room. On the graph page, the insights and preview panels had a fixed width and couldn't be resized at all.

- **Main layout (`app-layout.tsx`):** removed the 400px and 50% limits. Each panel can now grow until the center area reaches its 120px minimum. The minimum panel widths stay at 150px (left) and 250px (right). The left sidebar now opens at a third of the window width (at least 150px) instead of 220px, because at 220px most source and page names were cut off.
- **Graph page (`graph-view.tsx`):** the insights panel (default 320px, minimum 240px) and the preview panel (default 420px, minimum 320px) are now resizable. Each panel's limit accounts for the other one.
- **Shared handle (`panel-resize-handle.tsx`):** one drag handle replaces the drag code in the layout and is reused on the graph page. It uses pointer capture and can also be moved with the arrow keys, since it has `role="separator"`.
- **Translations:** added `layout.resizePanel` in en, it, ru and zh.

Panels are also capped with a CSS `max-width`, so a panel can't push the center area off screen when the window shrinks.

## Behaviour notes

- Panel widths still aren't saved between sessions.
- The graph redraws its canvas when a panel drag ends, based on the `panelResizing` flag on the document body. The new handle sets the same flag, so the graph panels trigger that redraw too.

## Testing

- Mock test suite, `tsc` and `vite build` all pass.

Fixes #827.

activity.title: Re-ingest shortens single-source pages and creates duplicates
activity.body:
**Version:** v0.6.13

I re-ingested 3 sources in a wiki of about 1,400 pages, to recover pages an earlier ingest had dropped. It did add the missing pages, but it also damaged existing ones in two ways. I've opened a PR for each, but both change behaviour you may have chosen on purpose, so this issue is the place to discuss the approach.

## 1. Re-ingest silently shortens pages owned by a single source

`ingest.ts` sets `replaceExistingBody` when a page's only source is the one being ingested, and `mergePageContent` then swaps in the new body without an LLM merge. I can see why: a corrected source should be able to replace its own pages.

The problem is that the new body is a fresh summary, and it can be much shorter even when the source hasn't changed. In my run, these 5 pages each lost 26–39% of their body:

| Page | Body before | Body after |
|---|---:|---:|
| regression-vs-matching-vs-propensity-score | 2,046 | 1,254 |
| quantile-regression | 2,547 | 1,574 |
| cluster-robust-standard-errors | 2,069 | 1,341 |
| difference-in-differences | 2,371 | 1,552 |
| two-stage-least-squares | 2,728 | 2,008 |

Sections such as Inputs, Steps and Assumptions disappeared, along with reported figures. The only trace I found is a recovery copy in `.llm-wiki/page-history`; nothing tells the user a page shrank.

**PR:** #838 replaces a page only when the recorded source hash differs, so a corrected source still replaces its pages.

## 2. The model can't see most existing pages, so it creates duplicates

`wiki/index.md` is the page list given to the model, but in my wiki it only shows the most recent pages:

- `updateBoundedRecentIndexSection` keeps 200 entries in "Recently Updated".
- The type sections (Entities, Concepts and so on) are all empty, and the prompt tells the model not to write the index.
- So 200 of about 1,400 pages were listed, and nothing else in the index links to the rest.

Re-ingesting created 9 duplicates under slightly different slugs, for example `regression-discontinuity` next to the existing `regression-discontinuity-design`, and `hc-robust-standard-errors` next to `heteroskedasticity-robust-standard-errors`. Each page I checked in a pair was missing from the index. A complete index wouldn't solve this at this size, because it would have to fit within `WIKI_INDEX_PROMPT_MAX_CHARS` (32,000).

I first tried comparing new pages with every page on disk, and measured some rules against the wiki while it still contained those 9 pairs:

| Rule | Known pairs caught | Other matches |
|---|---:|---:|
| Same type and title | 1 of 9 | 2 |
| Same type and a shared long alias | 2 of 9 | 25 |
| Same type and source, title overlap of at least 50% | 6 of 9 | 15 |

The other matches include real duplicates such as `imf` and `international-monetary-fund`, but also different topics, such as `value-at-risk` and `conditional-value-at-risk`. That's too unreliable for merging pages automatically.

All 9 pairs came from the same source, though, and a source has only about 22 pages (52 at most in my wiki).

**PR:** #839 adds two lists to the generation prompt: the pages already citing this source, and existing pages from other sources whose names appear in the analysis. It asks the model to reuse those paths for the same topics.

The second list covers duplicates across different sources. In a test run of four overlapping sources, 7 pages were shared between them, against 1 in my old wiki. Details and caveats are in #839.

## What I didn't verify

I worked this out from reading the code and comparing the wiki before and after. I didn't capture the actual prompts from these runs, so the link between the index and the duplicates is an inference, though a strong one. I've since run both PRs together on four sources with one model, as described in #839. That's a small test, and it can't separate the effect of each PR.

  `implement-spec` (user-invoked) implements a whole spec in one run. It reads the tickets as a **task graph**, runs implementer subagents in their own worktrees across the ready **frontier**, and lands everything on one **integration branch**, closing out with `code-review`. Ahead of graduating:

  - The goal is now the integration branch, not a PR. A draft PR opens only when the issue tracker closes work through PRs or you ask for one, and only after the first merge (a branch with no commits ahead of main can't open one). Without a PR, the tickets are resolved the way the tracker closes work.
  - It points at the issue tracker like its siblings, telling you to run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills` when none has been provided, rather than silently defaulting to `gh`.

- [#1120](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/pull/1120) [`2aecca1`](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/commit/2aecca12ea9ff047f76c8178cb64dfeafd192abe) Thanks [@mattpocock](https://github.com/mattpocock)! - Graduate **`pr`** into the **Engineering** bucket, so it ships in the Claude Code plugin, gets a docs page, and is routed by `ask-matt` as the PR-body close-out.

  `pr` (model-invoked) is the shape a pull request body should take: a summary as the smallest visual that makes the change clear (pseudocode, a call tree, a file tree, Mermaid, a diff), before/after evidence that it works, and a merge-danger call (one-way or two-way door, plus blast radius). The Summary visuals are adapted from Dex Horthy's `show-me`, credited in the skill's `CREDITS.md`.

- [#1120](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/pull/1120) [`2aecca1`](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/commit/2aecca12ea9ff047f76c8178cb64dfeafd192abe) Thanks [@mattpocock](https://github.com/mattpocock)! - Graduate **`retro`** into the **Engineering** bucket, so it ships in the Claude Code plugin, gets a docs page, and is routed by `ask-matt` as the last step of the main flow, after `code-review`.

  `retro` (user-invoked) looks back at a coding session and suggests changes to the agent's environment rather than the code: navigation pointers, automated checks, coding standards, steering files, tool economy, information access. It classifies each coding-standards finding first: a mechanical violation gets a deterministic check (a linter rule, a pre-commit hook, or a CI job), and `CODING_STANDARDS.md` is kept for genuine judgement calls. A repo with no guardrail at all is a finding in its own right.

- [#1120](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/pull/1120) [`daa01d8`](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/commit/daa01d8aa68ad5c61b68970ec2018d0ce9567be6) Thanks [@mattpocock](https://github.com/mattpocock)! - Remove the **`resolving-merge-conflicts`** skill. It's no longer needed, and nothing replaces it: the agent works through an in-progress merge or rebase conflict without a dedicated skill. It leaves the Claude Code plugin, the README and the `ask-matt` router. Its docs page at `https://aihero.dev/skills-resolving-merge-conflicts` stays up, marked archived.

- [#1120](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/pull/1120) [`006a52b`](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/commit/006a52be23e0178375e083e30535fa8224471f3e) Thanks [@mattpocock](https://github.com/mattpocock)! - Rename the `CONTEXT.md`/`CONTEXT-MAP.md` domain-doc convention to `GLOSSARY.md`/`GLOSSARY-MAP.md` everywhere the skills read and write it (`domain-modeling`, `grill-with-docs`, `improve-codebase-architecture`, `setup-matt-pocock-skills`, `triage`, `tdd`, `diagnosing-bugs`, `ask-matt`, `codebase-design`, `wait-what`, `pr`), plus the docs pages and this repo's own root glossary.

  If you have an existing `CONTEXT.md` (or `CONTEXT-MAP.md`) from before this change, `git mv` it to the new name: the skills only look for `GLOSSARY.md`/`GLOSSARY-MAP.md` going forward.

### Patch Changes

- [#848](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/pull/848) [`f02e2ed`](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/commit/f02e2ed3624d031272f8547742d23bf6bca8b072) Thanks [@mattpocock](https://github.com/mattpocock)! - domain-modeling: trigger on discussing codebase terminology and on writing or editing a GLOSSARY.md or an ADR directly, replacing the narrower "pin down domain terminology or a ubiquitous language" / "record an architectural decision" phrasing. Also drops the "another skill needs to maintain the domain model" caveat, since that's the invoking skill's job to state explicitly, not this description's.

An unquoted colon-space left over from the em-dash sweep in [#905](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/issues/905) made each block invalid YAML, so `skills.sh` skipped all six during discovery and they couldn't be listed or installed via `npx skills`.

- [#917](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/pull/917) [`85f83d3`](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/commit/85f83d3fde1d3a90d5c9a657f6998c79a6c37308) Thanks [@mattpocock](https://github.com/mattpocock)! - grilling: update the round template so consecutive questions are separated by a horizontal rule (`---`) instead of running together.

- [#879](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/pull/879) [`d419977`](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/commit/d419977fe07d9e1607d3523f3579310bbb076b93) Thanks [@mattpocock](https://github.com/mattpocock)! - grilling: remove em-dashes from `SKILL.md`, replacing them with colons and semicolons so the instructions read as plain text.

- [#905](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/pull/905) [`e6e9577`](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/commit/e6e957797d8cceb5b351c0dc840369523f9fb8fb) Thanks [@mattpocock](https://github.com/mattpocock)! - Remove every em-dash from the repo's prose (docs, `SKILL.md` files, ADRs, `README.md`, scripts, JSON/YAML metadata), hand-rewriting each sentence with a comma, colon, period, parentheses, or conjunction rather than mechanically substituting the character. `CLAUDE.md`/`AGENTS.md` now says not to reintroduce them.

- [#878](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/pull/878) [`e3e547b`](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/commit/e3e547b57d549110a0aa6ff40fd7b871c01c76c9) Thanks [@mattpocock](https://github.com/mattpocock)! - Standardize cross-skill invocation on an explicit "call the Skill tool" instruction instead of bare `/skill`-style prose, across `code-review`, `diagnosing-bugs`, `grill-with-docs`, `grill-me`, `improve-codebase-architecture`, `tdd`, `to-spec`, `to-tickets`, `triage`, and `wayfinder`.

  - A skill that names another skill in prose ("run the `/grilling` skill") does not reliably cause it to load. This is the documented rough edge behind `grill-with-docs`'s most-reported problem. Naming the tool directly (`Call the Skill tool with "grilling"`) is intended to raise the hit rate. Dropping the leading `/` also makes the instruction harness-neutral rather than less: it no longer assumes Claude Code's trigger syntax.
  - A step needing more than one skill now says so as multiple calls ("Call the Skill tool twice, for `grilling` and `domain-modeling`"), not one call carrying two names.
  - Documents the convention in `.agents/invocation.md` for future skills to follow.

- [#880](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/pull/880) [`1dab982`](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/commit/1dab98299c3b81f560026c01b7ebf55ed5d91373) Thanks [@mattpocock](https://github.com/mattpocock)! - Stop skills from trying to reach user-invoked skills through the Skill tool: fix cross-skill references that violated the "no other skill can call it" invariant in `.agents/invocation.md`, in `to-spec`, `wayfinder`, `to-tickets`, `triage`, `code-review`, and `diagnosing-bugs`.

  - `to-spec`, `wayfinder`, `to-tickets`, `triage`, and `code-review` each carried a precondition ("...run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills` if not") that PR [#878](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/issues/878) rewrote into a literal `Call the Skill tool with "setup-matt-pocock-skills"` instruction. `setup-matt-pocock-skills` is user-invoked, so none of these skills (user-invoked or model-invoked) can call it. Reworded all five as instructions for the agent to tell the human to run it instead.
  - `diagnosing-bugs`'s Phase 6 post-mortem hand off to `improve-codebase-architecture` (also user-invoked) the same way, from an autonomous, often-unattended bug-fixing flow with no human in the loop to catch the failed call. Removed the hand-off outright rather than softening it, since it rarely fired in practice. Phase 6 is now "Cleanup" only; the mechanical checklist is untouched.
  - Added a carve-out paragraph to `.agents/invocation.md`'s "Dependencies between them" section: the `Call the Skill tool with "name"` convention only applies when the named skill is model-invoked. This is the section PR [#878](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/issues/878) introduced without reconciling it against the user-invoked/model-invoked invariant stated eight lines above it; the gap is most of why this bug reached six call sites instead of one.

  Fixes [#453](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/issues/453).

- [#904](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/pull/904) [`594f0f8`](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/commit/594f0f83188921a60d45d63d6cdac509de20df2c) Thanks [@mattpocock](https://github.com/mattpocock)! - wait-what: follow `GLOSSARY-MAP.md` to the right `GLOSSARY.md` when a repo indexes multiple contexts that way instead of keeping a single root `GLOSSARY.md`.

- [#1121](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/pull/1121) [`c5b9869`](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/commit/c5b98691982c4f0d3a5e40ab09566b3b84721e00) Thanks [@mattpocock](https://github.com/mattpocock)! - `ask-matt` no longer says `diagnosing-bugs` hands off to `improve-codebase-architecture` from a post-mortem; that step was removed. It now points you at `/retro` once the fix is in, to ask what would have prevented the bug, and at `/improve-codebase-architecture` where the finding is a missing seam. The `diagnosing-bugs` docs page drops the same stale hand-off. Thanks @Ygilany for spotting it ([#1117](https://github.com/mattpocock/skills/issues/1117)).

activity.title: implement-spec: resolved tickets keep ready-for-agent labels and ticket debris after the run
activity.body:
## Problem

`skills/engineering/implement-spec/SKILL.md` step 8 says:

> resolve each ticket the way the issue tracker closes work

Closing an issue does not remove its labels. So after `/implement-spec` finishes, every resolved ticket still carries the `ready-for-agent` label — the exact signal that means "agent-grabbable". Step 9 then says only:

> 9. Clean up all **implementer subagent** worktrees.

…which leaves the ticket branches, the merged integration branch, and (on a local tracker) the `.scratch/<feature>/` ticket files untouched. The skill resolves tickets but never closes out the *signals* around them: closed ≠ done.

## Steps to reproduce / observed

Two repos, two tracker kinds, same residue after multiple `/implement-spec` runs:

- **GitHub tracker**: 19 closed issues, all still labeled `ready-for-agent`. `to-tickets` applies that label on publish; nothing ever removes it.
- **Local markdown tracker**: `.scratch/<feature>/issues/*.md` still read `Status: ready-for-agent` with every acceptance checkbox unticked, months after the spec itself was archived as "已实施 (implemented)". Part of this is vocabulary: `triage-labels.md` defines five state roles and no terminal one, and `issue-tracker-local.md` has no `done` state for implementation tickets — so there is nowhere to *record* that a ticket finished.
- In both cases, `ticket/NN-*` branches and the already-merged integration branch also survived (adjacent to #1251, which covers the *mechanics* of deleting them under guardrails — this issue is about the *duty*).

## Why it matters

- `ready-for-agent` on a closed issue is stale state that misleads humans scanning the tracker, and any tooling that filters by label rather than by state.
- Local ticket files claiming `ready-for-agent` + unticked criteria contradict the archived spec that says the work shipped.
- Debris accumulates per run, so the cost grows with every spec.

## Proposed wording

Step 8, appended:

```text
When a ticket is resolved, also remove its `ready-for-agent` label (on a
local tracker: set `Status: done` and tick the acceptance criteria) — a
closed ticket must not still look agent-grabbable.
```

Step 9, extended:

```text
9. Clean up all **implementer subagent** worktrees, delete the merged
ticket branches and the integration branch, and archive the finished
local ticket directory (`.scratch/<feature>/` → `.scratch/archive/`).
```

The local-tracker half may additionally need a terminal state to exist in `issue-tracker-local.md` / `triage-labels.md`, otherwise there is no legitimate `Status:` value for step 8 to set.

## Related

- #1251 — step 9 branch-deletion mechanics under guardrails (how to delete; this issue is what to delete)
- #292 — the mirror image at the front of the lifecycle: a parent staying pickable after decomposition

```text
description: Shared language for designing a software factory: the tasks it run…
```

```yaml
name: software-factory
```

```diff
---
name: software-factory
-description: Shared language for designing a software factory: the tasks it runs and the services it plugs into.
+description: "Shared language for designing a software factory: the tasks it runs and the services it plugs into."
disable-model-invocation: true
---
```

activity.title: Remove the harness-specific Skill tool dependency from grill-me and grill-with-docs

`grill-me`:
> Call the Skill tool with "grilling".

`grill-with-docs`:
> Call the Skill tool twice, for "grilling" and "domain-modeling".

Some harnesses use a different activation mechanism or load skills by reading their files directly. In those environments, these instructions cannot be followed literally, even when the referenced skills are available.

Replace the tool-specific instructions with explicit instructions to read and follow their dependencies.

For `grill-me/SKILL.md`:

```md
Read and follow `../grilling/SKILL.md` before starting the interview.

Resolve this path relative to the directory containing this SKILL.md.
```

```md
Read and follow both skills before starting the interview:

- `../grilling/SKILL.md`
- `../domain-modeling/SKILL.md`

Resolve these paths relative to the directory containing this SKILL.md.
```

This preserves the intended composition without requiring a particular tool or duplicating the underlying instructions. Specifying the path base also avoids resolving the references against the agent’s working directory.

## Problem

The official v1.3.1 tree (`24fe0ef7737efae15c87225755e9f6f5965e4888`) has 37 `SKILL.md` directories and the MIT notice at the repository root, but no package-local LICENSE/NOTICE files.

Would you consider shipping the unchanged root MIT LICENSE inside each independently distributable skill directory, or documenting another supported package-local notice mechanism? This would let subdirectory consumers retain the original notice and follow upstream updates without a locally maintained adaptation.

The proposed notice is byte-identical to the root LICENSE; no changes to SKILL.md, resources, authorship claims, or consumer permissions are requested. I have not modified this repository or submitted a patch. A solution at the publisher packaging boundary would be preferable to custom downstream installers.

In line 696, `check_dangling_signature_id(new_expr)` executes this pattern against the **entire transformed CEL expression string**:

```python
if check_dangling_signature_id(new_expr):
  dangling_id_detected = True
```

##### Impact
- **False Flagging of Valid Rules:** If a custom Common Expression Language (CEL) rule evaluates HTTP attributes or custom query parameters containing `id<digits>` (e.g., `request.headers['id99999']` or `inIpRange(origin.ip, '10.0.0.0/8')`), the parser treats the digits as an OWASP CRS signature number.
- **Premature Upgrade Blocking:** Because the extracted identifier does not belong to the CRS 4.22 catalog, the script marks `dangling_id_detected = True`, generating false warning logs and incorrectly advising operators to purge valid rule conditions.

##### Recommended Remediation
Scope the signature check strictly to arguments inside `evaluatePreconfiguredWaf()` calls rather than evaluating the entire expression string.

---

#### B. False Negative in Google SecOps YARA-L 2.0 Rule Validator

- **Finding Category:** False Negative (Missed Detection)
- **Affected File:** [`skills/cloud/secops-detection-engineering/scripts/validate_yaral_rule.py`](file:///d:/Antigravity/fork/google_skills/skills/cloud/secops-detection-engineering/scripts/validate_yaral_rule.py#L92-L94) (Lines 92–94)

##### Description
The YARA-L validator enforces syntax rules for CIDR Reference Lists, where IP comparison against CIDR lists requires the explicit `in cidr` operator. The validation pattern is defined as:

```python
CIDR_BARE_LIST_RE = re.compile(
    r"\.\s*(?:ip|nat_ip)\s+in\s+%[A-Za-z0-9_]*cidr[A-Za-z0-9_]*\b"
)
```

##### Impact
- **Incomplete Syntax Enforcement:** The validator relies solely on the string `"cidr"` being present in the reference list name (`%...cidr...`).
- **Compiler Failures in Production:** If a security analyst uses standard enterprise list names that omit the literal word `"cidr"` (e.g., `$e.src.ip in %corp_internal_subnets` or `%rfc1918_networks`), the validator **fails to detect** the missing `cidr` modifier. The rule passes local linting but fails abruptly upon submission to the Google SecOps detection engine compiler.

##### Recommended Remediation
Track declared reference list types semantically or parse list metadata definitions instead of relying on naming conventions.

---

#### C. False Positive / Least Privilege Inversion in IAM Troubleshooting Helper

- **Finding Category:** False Positive / Flawed Logic (Privilege Inversion)
- **Affected File:** [`skills/cloud/iam-helper-for-troubleshooting/scripts/least_privileged_role.py`](file:///d:/Antigravity/fork/google_skills/skills/cloud/iam-helper-for-troubleshooting/scripts/least_privileged_role.py#L109-L132) (Lines 109–132)

##### Description
The utility `find_least_privileged_role()` is designed to identify the role with the fewest permissions that satisfies a specific API operation. However, the candidate role sorting key is defined as:

```python
valid_roles.sort(
    key=lambda x: (
        not x["is_service_level_standard"],
        not x["is_predefined"],
        x["perm_count"],
    )
)
```

Where `is_service_level_standard` explicitly checks for roles ending in administrative suffixes:

```python
is_service_level_standard = role_name.startswith("roles/") and (
    role_name_lower.endswith("admin")
    or role_name_lower.endswith("editor")
    or role_name_lower.endswith("viewer")
    or role_name_lower.endswith("reader")
    or role_name_lower.endswith("writer")
)
```

##### Impact
- **Recommending Administrative Roles as "Least Privileged":** Because `not x["is_service_level_standard"]` is evaluated before `x["perm_count"]`, any standard service role ending in `admin` (e.g., `roles/storage.admin` with dozens of destructive permissions) is sorted **ahead** of a tightly scoped predefined role (e.g., `roles/storage.objectViewer` or custom task-specific roles) that lacks the `"admin"` suffix.
- **Misleading Security Recommendations:** Users following the script's recommendations under the assumption of implementing least privilege will inadvertently assign broad administrative capabilities to workloads and users.

##### Recommended Remediation
Prioritize raw `perm_count` ascending first, and penalize administrative role suffixes (`admin`, `editor`) rather than boosting them in the least-privilege calculation.

activity.title: Insecure Invocation of Legacy Tooling in Maintenance Mode (`gsutil`)
activity.body:
### Insecure Invocation of Legacy Tooling in Maintenance Mode (`gsutil`)

- **Severity:** Low / Security Hygiene
- **Vulnerability Type:** Deprecated / Obsolete Component Usage (CWE-1104: Use of Unmaintained Third-Party Components)
- **Affected File:** [`skills/cloud/agent-platform-eval-flywheel/scripts/endpoint_evaluation.py`](file:///d:/Antigravity/fork/google_skills/skills/cloud/agent-platform-eval-flywheel/scripts/endpoint_evaluation.py#L117-L122) (Lines 117–122)

##### Description
The evaluation script invokes `gsutil` via a subprocess call to read dataset files stored in Google Cloud Storage:

```python
try:
  jsonl_content = subprocess.run(
      ["gsutil", "cat", dataset],
      capture_output=True,
      text=True,
      check=True,
  ).stdout
except subprocess.CalledProcessError as e:
  raise RuntimeError(f"Error reading dataset from {dataset}.") from e
```

Google Cloud has officially transitioned `gsutil` into **maintenance mode**, directing all development, performance optimizations, and security updates to `gcloud storage` and the official client libraries.

##### Impact
- **Maintenance & Compatibility Risks:** `gsutil` receives only critical bug fixes and does not support modern Google Cloud Storage capabilities (e.g., advanced gRPC transport, enhanced object retention configurations, or newer IAM authentication paradigms).
- **Subprocess Execution Overhead:** Invoking an external Python-based binary (`gsutil`) via `subprocess.run` inside a script introduces unnecessary process-spawning overhead, brittle exit code handling, and potential pipeline failures in environments where `gsutil` is omitted from modern container images.
- **Inconsistent Credential Resolution:** Relying on `gsutil` subprocess authentication can cause discrepancies when running under Workload Identity Federation or short-lived service account tokens compared to native SDK calls.

##### Recommended Remediation
Migrate from `gsutil cat` to the official `google-cloud-storage` Python SDK for robust in-process execution, or switch to the modern `gcloud storage` CLI:

1. **Option 1: Native Python Client Library (Recommended)**
   ```python
   from google.cloud import storage

   def read_gcs_dataset(gcs_uri: str) -> str:
       # Parses gs://bucket_name/path/to/blob
       bucket_name, blob_path = gcs_uri.replace("gs://", "").split("/", 1)
       client = storage.Client()
       bucket = client.bucket(bucket_name)
       blob = bucket.blob(blob_path)
       return blob.download_as_text()
   ```

2. **Option 2: CLI Replacement with `gcloud storage`**
   ```python
   subprocess.run(
       ["gcloud", "storage", "cat", dataset],
       capture_output=True,
       text=True,
       check=True,
   )
   ```

activity.body:
### Overly Permissive IAM Recommendations (Violation of Least Privilege)

- **Severity:** Medium
- **Vulnerability Type:** Insecure Default / Excessive Privileges (CWE-272: Least Privilege Violation / CWE-250: Execution with Unnecessary Privileges)
- **Affected File:** [`skills/cloud/application-integration-basics/SKILL.md`](file:///d:/Antigravity/fork/google_skills/skills/cloud/application-integration-basics/SKILL.md#L94) (Line 94)

##### Description
The setup and onboarding instructions for Google Cloud Application Integration advise operators to grant broad, project-level primitive roles:

> *"Setting up Application Integration requires `roles/integrations.integrationAdmin`, `roles/connectors.admin`, and `roles/editor` (plus `roles/cloudkms.admin` for CMEK). Check current bindings (read-only):"*

##### Impact
- **Breach of Least Privilege Principle:** Granting `roles/editor` provides broad read and modify permissions across almost all Google Cloud services in the project (including Cloud Storage, Compute Engine, BigQuery, Cloud Functions, and Pub/Sub).
- **Expanded Blast Radius:** If credentials or automated identities provisioned following this guidance are compromised, attackers can pivot across unrelated project workloads rather than remaining scoped to Application Integration assets.
- **Compliance & Audit Failures:** Modern cloud security standards (such as CIS Google Cloud Platform Foundation Benchmark) explicitly flag project-wide primitive roles (`roles/editor` and `roles/owner`) as critical audit findings.

##### Recommended Remediation
1. **Remove Primitive Role Requirement:** Replace `roles/editor` with granular predefined roles required exclusively by Application Integration and its connectors (e.g., `roles/integrations.admin`, `roles/connectors.admin`, and specific service agent permissions).
2. **Audit Service Account Grants:** Ensure identities running the integrations only receive permissions at the resource or connector level rather than at the project boundary.

activity.title: Arbitrary Code Execution via `eval()` with Dynamic String Concatenation
activity.body:
### Arbitrary Code Execution via `eval()` with Dynamic String Concatenation

- **Severity:** High
- **Vulnerability Type:** Code Injection (CWE-95: Improper Neutralization of Directives in Dynamically Evaluated Code)
- **Affected File:** [`skills/cloud/apigee-agent-gateway-governance/scripts/assess_integration.sh`](file:///d:/Antigravity/fork/google_skills/skills/cloud/apigee-agent-gateway-governance/scripts/assess_integration.sh#L163-L171) (Lines 163–171, 479–480)

##### Description
The shell utility function `jqf()` is designed to extract JSON properties without requiring a native `jq` binary by spawning a Python inline script that executes `eval(sys.argv[1])`:

```bash
jqf() {  # jqf <json> <python-expr over d> -- no jq dependency
  python3 -c '
import json,sys
try: d=json.loads(sys.stdin.read() or "{}")
except Exception: d={}
try: print(eval(sys.argv[1]))
except Exception: print("")
' "$1" 2>/dev/null || true
}
```

In lines 479–480 of the same script, the dynamically resolved shell variable `CACHE_INDEX_ID` is interpolated directly into the Python expression using string concatenation:

```bash
CACHE_DIMS="$(jqf 'next((str(i.get("metadata",{}).get("config",{}).get("dimensions","")) for i in d if i["name"].endswith("'"$CACHE_INDEX_ID"'")), "")' <<<"$IDX_JSON")"
```

##### Impact
Because `$CACHE_INDEX_ID` is concatenated directly into the Python code string without escaping or input validation, any single quote (`'`) present in the index identifier breaks out of the string boundary. This allows arbitrary Python code execution under the privileges of the script runner when processing untrusted, malformed, or hostile index names.

##### Recommended Remediation
1. **Eliminate `eval()`**: Replace the dynamic evaluation with safe dictionary lookups passed via explicit arguments or environment variables.
2. **Dedicated CLI JSON Parsing**: If `jq` is unavailable, write a dedicated, parameter-safe Python helper script that parses JSON paths without executing arbitrary Python statements:

```bash
jqf_safe() {
  python3 -c '
import json, sys
try:
    data = json.load(sys.stdin)
    target_id = sys.argv[1]
    for item in data:
        if item.get("name", "").endswith(target_id):
            print(item.get("metadata", {}).get("config", {}).get("dimensions", ""))
            break
except Exception:
    pass
' "$CACHE_INDEX_ID" <<<"$IDX_JSON"
}
```

activity.title: add-companions-and-sarif
Require verbatim quotes in trace/evidence and check them with --target (#134)
activity.body:
Fixes #134.

## Problem

Trace and evidence entries cite a `file` and `line` but contain no source bytes. The validator never reads the target, so it cannot tell a real citation from an invented one. Main has no `--target` option.

The reproduction on main at c1c8a8c uses a `confirmed` SQL-injection record that has every field the schema requires. Its trace and evidence are:

```json
"trace": [
  {"kind": "entrypoint",  "file": "skills/security-audit/report-schema.json", "line": 1, "scope": "getUser",    "description": "req.query.id enters the handler."},
  {"kind": "propagation", "file": "skills/security-audit/report-schema.json", "line": 2, "scope": "buildQuery", "description": "id is concatenated into the SQL text."},
  {"kind": "sink",        "file": "skills/security-audit/report-schema.json", "line": 3, "scope": "db.query",   "description": "The concatenated SQL is executed."}
],
"evidence": [
  {"file": "LICENSE", "line": 1, "description": "The query is built by string concatenation."}
]
```

Called directly, `validateDocument([record], schema)` reports no errors, and the CLI passes the same document:

```
validateDocument(findings, schema): 0 error(s)
CLI: node validate-findings.cjs <tmp>/findings.json -> exit 0
  PASS: 1 findings valid
```

## Change

- In `report-schema.json`, every `trace[]` and `evidence[]` item, in all three branches, requires `quote`. It must be a string with at least one visible character, as the existing `visibleContent` rule requires. The validator never trims or normalizes its value. As with `fingerprint`, only the `confirmed` branch includes the field's description.
- `validate-findings.cjs`:
  - Adds an opt-in `--target <target-dir>` flag and a matching `validateDocument(findings, schema, { target })` option. With a target, the validator reads each cited file from below the target. Each quote must match the file's bytes starting on the cited line. A quote starts on a line when its first byte is a byte of that line, including the line's LF. Newlines in a quote continue it onto the following lines. The validator counts lines by LF. It compares UTF-8 bytes, so CRLF does not match LF, and NFC does not match NFD.
  - The validator checks quotes in every verdict: `confirmed`, `needs_validation`, and `rejected`.
  - Cited paths must still pass the existing lexical check, which rejects absolute and `..` paths. The validator also rejects any path that is a symlink or passes through one. It checks that `realpath` equals the joined path. It opens the leaf with `O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK`, and the leaf must be a regular file. This reuses the existing hardened input reader, which now reads both the findings input and target files. Its existing messages are unchanged.
  - The validator rejects a cited file over 64 MiB. It reads each cited file once and searches for each quote only within the cited line plus the quote's length. Quote checks read and search at most 512 MiB in total. Without that cap, the validator would repeat the same work for many citations of one long line, or for citations of many hard links to one large file. For example, 2,000 citations of a 16 MiB one-line file took 36 s before the cap, and the validator now rejects them in under 1 s. Errors stay in document order and under the existing 100-message cap.
  - The CLI usage is `validate-findings.cjs <path-to-findings.json> [--target <target-dir>]`. The parser also accepts `--target` before the findings path. It accepts exactly one findings path and at most one `--target <dir>`. For anything else, it prints usage and exits 1, so a typo like `--taget` fails the run instead of skipping the check. If the target is unusable, the CLI fails with `Failed to read target: target must be an existing directory`.
- Docs:
  - `VALIDATION-AND-REPORTING.md` defines `quote` and says the validator checks quotes in every verdict, `rejected` included. Its validator command is now `validate-findings.cjs <output-dir>/findings.json --target <target>`. It also says what a pass does and does not prove. The Phase 3 and Phase 5 verifier checklists now include the quote.
  - `HUNTING.md` asks hunters for quotes.
  - `SKILL.md` covers prior records without quotes. See Compatibility.

The change adds these messages:

```
$[0].trace[0]: missing required field "quote"
$[0].trace[0].quote: must match the bytes of "src/db.js" starting on line 5
$[0].trace[0].line: exceeds the last line of "src/db.js"
$[0].trace[0].file: cited file does not exist in the target
$[0].trace[0].file: cited file must not be or pass through a symlink
$[0].trace[0].file: cited file must be a regular file
$[0].trace[0].file: cited file exceeds 67108864 byte limit
$: quote checks exceed 536870912 byte limit
```

After the change, the reproduction above fails even without a target:

```
validateDocument(findings, schema): 5 error(s)
  $[0]: must match exactly one schema in oneOf; matched 0
  $[0].trace[0]: missing required field "quote"
  $[0].trace[1]: missing required field "quote"
  $[0].trace[2]: missing required field "quote"
  $[0].evidence[0]: missing required field "quote"
CLI: node validate-findings.cjs <tmp>/findings.json -> exit 1
  ...
  FAIL: 5 validation error(s)
```

With invented SQL quotes added, it fails under `--target`:

```
node validate-findings.cjs <tmp>/findings.json --target <repo> -> exit 1
  ERROR: $[0].trace[0].quote: must match the bytes of "skills/security-audit/report-schema.json" starting on line 1
  ERROR: $[0].trace[1].quote: must match the bytes of "skills/security-audit/report-schema.json" starting on line 2
  ERROR: $[0].trace[2].quote: must match the bytes of "skills/security-audit/report-schema.json" starting on line 3
  ERROR: $[0].evidence[0].quote: must match the bytes of "LICENSE" starting on line 1
  FAIL: 4 validation error(s)
```

## Relationship to #97

#97 adds a flag with the same name and meaning. In both PRs, `--target <dir>` is the checkout that repository-relative paths resolve under. The two PRs check different things.

- For every record that is not rejected, #97 checks that each claimed path exists under the target: `trace[].file`, `evidence[].file`, and `remediation.code_changes[].file_name`. It runs the check from the CLI, not from `validateDocument`.
- This PR checks that each trace and evidence quote's bytes start on the cited line, which also requires the file and the line to exist. It does not check `remediation.code_changes[].file_name`. That check is only in #97.
- This PR also checks `rejected` records, which reverses #97's exemption. A rejected record suppresses its claim in later runs, and main's docs define rejected records as source-grounded candidates. If both PRs land, the merge has to invert or drop #97's test "--target does not ground-truth rejected findings".
- If both land, the validator should check trace and evidence existence once. With both checks, a missing file gets two errors at the same location, with different wording. This PR's check is the stricter one, so #97 could limit its check to `remediation.code_changes[].file_name`.
- The documented order, `<findings> --target <target>`, works with both parsers. #97's CLI exits 1 when `--target` comes before the findings path.

The two PRs conflict in `validate-findings.cjs` and its test file. A conflict resolution has been validated locally only; no resolution patch has been published. It keeps one trace and evidence check and narrows #97's check to remediation file names. It also inverts #97's rejected test and updates the fixture and messages in #97's other two tests. All 86 tests pass on the merged tree. The resolution is not part of this PR.

## Compatibility

- The schema requires `quote` for every verdict. The three branches share one shape for trace and evidence items, and the docs describe all three as source-grounded. An invented citation does harm in each branch. `needs_validation` records go to owners, and `rejected` records suppress the same claim in later runs. A rejected record's trace is the claimed path through real code, so it has real lines to quote too.
- A `findings.json` written before this change fails validation with `missing required field "quote"`. The workflow reads prior runs while planning but does not re-validate their files. A carried record goes through the current verifier. The verifier returns a record in the current schema branch, so its quotes come from current source. `SKILL.md` now says that missing quotes alone do not make a prior file incompatible or a carried record ineligible. Without that sentence, the "evidence still meets the current contract" condition could drop old confirmed records.
- `--target` is opt-in, so shape-only validation still works where the target is not available. The documented Phase 4 command passes it, and Phase 5 reruns that command. Without `--target`, an invented quote passes, and a test asserts that behavior.
- `validateDocument(findings, schema)` still works because the third argument is optional. With `{ target }`, an unusable target makes it throw instead of returning an error.
- The CLI now rejects extra positional arguments and any `-` option other than `--target`. Previously, it ignored extra arguments.
- The change adds no dependencies. `LIMITS` gains `sourceFileBytes` and `quoteCheckBytes`. The coverage-ledger validator shares neither, so the helper-alignment test is unchanged.

## Limits

- A matching quote proves only that those bytes exist at the cited location in the checked-out tree. It does not prove the code is reachable, behaves as described, or is vulnerable. The issue's record still passes `--target` when its quotes are the real bytes of its cited lines: `{`, the `"$comment"` line, `"type": "array",` and `MIT License`. Establishing a claim is still the job of the independent verifiers in Phases 3 and 5.
- A short quote proves little. For example, `}` matches many lines. The check compares bytes at a location and does not judge relevance.
- The validator checks quotes against the tree as it is at run time, not against a commit.
- The symlink check is `realpath` followed by an `O_NOFOLLOW` open of the leaf. The validator does not detect a swap of an intermediate directory between the two calls, because Node has no `openat`-style walk. The target should be read-only during a run.
- The validator rejects symlinks inside the target too, so cite the real path. A quote can only hold UTF-8 text, so in a file that is not UTF-8, quote a UTF-8 fragment of the line.
- `--target` needs `O_NOFOLLOW` and `O_NONBLOCK`, which Node does not define on Windows. There, the CLI exits 1 with `Failed to read target: OS no-follow and nonblocking target protection is unavailable`, and `validateDocument(…, { target })` throws. The CLI loses no Windows support, because on main it already refuses to read the findings file on such platforms. Shape-only validation through `validateDocument(findings, schema)` still works there. The target tests skip when the flags are missing, and the symlink, FIFO and read-and-search cap tests also skip on `win32`. The tests ran only on Linux.

## Tests

The results below come from `node --test skills/security-audit/*.test.cjs` on Linux with Node v22.21.0. There is no package.json, and plain `node --test` from the repository root gives the same result.

- On main, all 65 tests pass and the run exits 0.
- On this branch, all 81 tests pass and the run exits 0. The findings suite grows from 34 to 50 tests, and the coverage-ledger suite stays at 31.
- With only `validate-findings.cjs` and `report-schema.json` reverted and the new tests and docs kept, 60 of 81 tests pass, 21 fail, and the run exits 1. The 21 failures are the 16 new tests plus 5 existing tests whose fixtures now include `quote`, which main rejects as an unexpected field.

The new tests cover:

- a missing quote in every verdict branch, including the issue's record
- empty, whitespace-only, invisible, lone-surrogate and non-string quotes
- tabs, CR and NUL in a quote, preserved exactly
- shape-only behavior without a target
- accepted quotes: whole line, mid-line fragment, multi-line, leading newline from an empty line, trailing LF, CRLF, non-ASCII
- rejected quotes: absent, on another line, starting on the previous line, running past the line, reindented, LF for CRLF, NFD for NFC
- a line past the end of the file, including `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`
- `../`, `src/../..` and absolute paths
- symlinks: leaf, directory, and inside the target
- missing and non-regular files, oversized sparse files, and a path through a file
- the read and search cap, with a 16 MiB line and with hard links to a 64 MiB file
- passing and failing CLI runs with `--target` after the findings path, the same check with `--target` first, malformed arguments, unusable targets, and a cited FIFO, which the CLI rejects without blocking
- quote checks in `rejected` and `needs_validation` records

Two tests cover the verdict rule: "--target checks quotes in rejected records too" and "--target checks quotes in needs_validation records too". Each builds its record from that verdict's fixture, asserts the verdict, and checks the CLI's exact stderr for a forged quote and a missing file. In a scratch copy of the validator that skips `needs_validation` records, only the second test fails. Before that test existed, no test caught the skip. A copy that skips `rejected` records, which is #97's rule, fails the first test and 7 others whose shared helper builds a rejected record.

Adding the missing skip options to these remaining seven tests aligns `validate-findings.test.cjs` with its sibling and ensures the test suite reports skipped tests rather than unexpected failures on platforms without safe-open flags.

activity.body:
Hi, we vendored the security-audit skill and ran its validators. We found two issues. Both are still present at c1c8a8c1.

### 1. An archived verifier's check can come back into the live state (validate-coverage-ledger.cjs)

`priorOwners` collects `attempt.agent_id` from archived attempts, and later attempts may not reuse those ids. Archived **checks** are not covered: the `agent_id` on an archived `check` (the verifier) is never added to any set. So a check made by a verifier whose attempt was archived can be copied into the live state, and the ledger still validates. That defeats the independence the archive is meant to enforce.

Suggested fix: collect archived check owners in their own set (for example `priorCheckOwners`). Reject any of those ids when it appears on a later attempt or a live check, and use the same error style as the existing `priorOwners` rejection. A fixture with an archived check whose `agent_id` reappears on a live check would pin it.

### 2. Seven CLI tests have no `HAS_SAFE_INPUT_OPEN` skip (validate-findings.test.cjs)

`HAS_SAFE_INPUT_OPEN` (line 18) gates the tests that depend on `O_NOFOLLOW` and related flags, and some tests already use `{ skip: !HAS_SAFE_INPUT_OPEN }`. These seven do not, but they also go through `readFileWithinLimit`. Where the flags are missing, that function rejects the input before the behavior under test is reached, so each test fails with a generic error instead of skipping:

- accepts a producer-shaped findings document through the CLI (line 164)
- CLI rejects input above the byte limit without an exception trace (375)
- CLI rejects invalid UTF-8 without replacement or an exception trace (383)
- CLI rejects lone-surrogate prose without changing payload semantics (445)
- CLI rejects Unicode format controls in source paths (455)
- CLI rejects input above the nesting-depth limit without an exception trace (507)
- CLI rejects an oversized array without an exception trace (516)

Suggested fix: add `{ skip: !HAS_SAFE_INPUT_OPEN }` to each, the same way lines 403 and 416 already do.

Happy to send a PR for either one if that helps.
